newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa reverses to end soft, seen in range.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa reverses to end soft, seen in range.

text.p: LIFFE cocoa futures gave back nearly all of its morning gains made on industry buying to end mostly softer on Tuesday, but traders expected cocoa to remain mainly rangebound in the near-term.
Origin sales emerged in late morning to help cocoa off morning highs and start prices drifting lower throughout the afternoon, traders said.
July closed down seven stg at 988 stg per tonne and September dropped seven to 1,004. December shed four to 998 after being as high as 1,016 in the morning.
Back-month industry buying from several firms helped lift cocoa to session highs early, traders said. But when the buying spree faded, traders said origin hedging emerged to bump prices lower.
Traders said crosses and against actuals (AAs) activity dominated while outright trading remained lackluster.

Total volume stood at 6,482 contracts, with March 1998 and December 1997 making up the bulk of trade. March 1998 led with 2,571 contracts changing hands while December garnered 1,115. Other months tallied less than 1,000 lots.

But traders noted market jitters reflected in a jumpy September/December spread. One trader said the spread traded as wide as 30 stg two weeks ago, halved last week, got down to about even and closed with September at a near six-stg premium from three at the midday break.
The swing in the spread showed underlying nervousness in the market, traders said.
Last week, the International Cocoa Organization and broker GNI cut estimates for this year's cocoa deficit due to upward revisions in the Ivorian crop.

Weather and crop analysts in Abdijan said on Tuesday continued rains across the region in late April were favourable to the mid-crop and early 1996/97 main crop. Forecasters expect the mid-crop to produce between 160,000 and 180,000 tonnes.
For the entire 1996/97 season, crop analysts expected it to close in on last year's record 1.2 million tonnes.
But many traders said a large Ivorian crop was already expected and priced into the market. Now, they expected cocoa to remain rangebound until actual Ivory Coast figures emerged.
Technically, cocoa also looked rangebound after July held key support last week at the April 9 low of 980 but could not muster the strength to pierce resistance at 1,008.
In options, no contracts changed hands.
